strapline: A last adjournment for Mundubile and Zulu, a one-horse race in Mandevu, inflation at 6.3 per cent, and an under-15 final in Baku

stories.title: 'This is the last adjournment': Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others appear at last, and the High Court sets 5 November for the bail hearing as the State asks for time to read the reply
stories.excerpt: All 18 applicants were brought from Mukobeko to the Lusaka High Court on Thursday 29 October, but the constitutional bail application still did not start. The Attorney-General asked for time to study the defence's 32-paragraph reply; the bench adjourned to 09:00 on Thursday 5 November and, the defence says, warned it would rule on the papers if either side was not ready. The State's affidavit argues two months in custody is not unreasonable for treason and terrorism charges and calls Mundubile and Zulu flight risks.

image.label: Fourth sitting, no hearing
image.caption: The constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others was adjourned for a fourth time at the Lusaka High Court on Thursday 29 October 2026, to 5 November.

body: The 18 men were in the building this time. A day after the Lusaka High Court ordered Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility to produce them, Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and their 16 co-applicants were brought to court on Thursday 29 October, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer reported. Their constitutional bail application still did not begin. The bench of Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga adjourned it to 09:00 on Thursday 5 November, and, according to the defence, told both sides that there would be no fifth postponement.

The reason this time was the paperwork. Zambia Monitor reported that the applicants had filed a 32-paragraph affidavit in reply and 13 paragraphs of skeleton arguments answering the State's opposition, and that Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha asked for time to study them. The State had first proposed 3 November, defence lawyer Milner Katolo told reporters, but the first and second applicants have another matter before a different judge that day. Katolo had argued against a fourth adjournment altogether, proposing that the court resume at 14:00 the same afternoon or on Friday morning.

body.text: The court has insisted and emphasised that this is the last adjournment.
body.attribution: Milner Katolo, lawyer for the applicants, to reporters outside the Lusaka High Court on Thursday 29 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body.text: We asked for more time to study it because it's bulky.
body.attribution: Mulilo Kabesha, Attorney-General, to reporters on Thursday 29 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Zambia Monitor's account of the court's position, as relayed by Katolo, is that any party not ready on 5 November will have the matter closed against it and a ruling made on the documents and arguments already filed, and that dates for the substantive petition will be set only after the bail ruling. The Zambian Observer reported that Thursday was the applicants' 63rd day in custody since their arrest on 27 August, and that they will have been held 70 days without trial by the time the court sits again. It quoted lead defence counsel Sakwiba Sikota as saying outside court that the clients have a constitutional right to bail and a speedy trial. The applicants were taken back to Mukobeko, in Kabwe, afterwards.

The State's written opposition, reported by Zambia Monitor early on Thursday, was sworn by Senior Superintendent Donald Mulimba, the officer in charge of Crime 1 at CID headquarters. It asks the court to dismiss the application with costs. Its core argument is that the charges, treason and offences under the anti-terrorism law, require extensive investigation, including digital forensics, financial evidence and cross-border enquiries, and that a delay of about two months is not unreasonable. It cites the Canadian case R v Morin, the Zambian case Shamwana v The People and a judgment of Zimbabwe's Constitutional Court, and it argues that the applicants have not shown prejudice from the delay.

The affidavit goes further on Mundubile and Zulu, the NRPUP's presidential candidate and running mate in August. It describes them as flight risks, alleging that they evaded arrest by going into the United Nations House, and it says their political influence creates a risk of interference with State witnesses. It adds that the offences carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment, that no bail conditions could guarantee attendance, and that detention is needed for public safety and national security. These are the State's allegations; none has been tested in court, and no trial has begun.

The application has now failed to start four times. On Wednesday 28 October, Zambia Monitor reported, the sitting collapsed because the applicants had not been brought from Mukobeko and could not sign the affidavit their lawyers had drafted overnight after receiving the State's response at about 17:00 on Tuesday. Chief State Advocate Chali Hambayi said then that the adjournment followed the defence's own request for time and that the State had met the agreed filing deadline. The court ordered all 18 to be produced at 10:00 on Thursday and warned that the officer in charge of the prison would have to appear in person to explain any failure.

Katolo also told reporters on Thursday that one applicant had missed several appointments with a specialist abroad and had been given medication without a medical review, and he pointed the court to paragraph 59 of the National Prosecutions Authority's manual, which, he said, recognises constitutional bail where trial has been delayed. The applicants, who include a business executive and three former commandos as well as the two politicians, argue that detention while investigations remain incomplete violates their constitutional rights, and ask for unconditional release or bail on reasonable conditions.

body.title: The dates
items: 27 August — the 18 are arrested; they have been at Mukobeko since
October — the application is filed; two sittings pass without a hearing
27 October (evening) — State files its affidavit in opposition
28 October — third sitting fails; applicants not produced; court orders them brought on Thursday
29 October — all 18 in court; adjourned to 5 November at 09:00, described as the last adjournment

body.confirmed: That all 18 applicants were brought to the Lusaka High Court on Thursday 29 October and the bail application was adjourned to 09:00 on 5 November (Zambia Monitor; Zambian Observer). That the State has filed an affidavit opposing bail, sworn by a senior CID officer, which asks for dismissal with costs (Zambia Monitor). That the applicants filed a 32-paragraph reply and skeleton arguments (Zambia Monitor, quoting defence counsel).
body.unverified: Everything in the State's affidavit is allegation: that the applicants are flight risks, that two of them evaded arrest at the UN House, that they might interfere with witnesses. The applicants' claim that their detention is unlawful is likewise untested. Whether the court will rule on the papers or hear argument on 5 November depends on both sides being ready; the court's warning was reported by the defence, not from a written order. The Zambian Observer gives one judge's first name as Charles; Zambia Monitor and earlier reports give Davies Chibwili, which this edition uses.

stories.title: One name left on the Mandevu ballot: all three of Adrian Banda's rivals withdraw a week before polling day, and the FDD's Daniel Chisenga says threats to his family forced him out
stories.excerpt: Letters dated Wednesday 28 October from the FDD's Daniel Chisenga, the Leadership Movement's candidate and the independent Daniel Daka reached the Electoral Commission a week before the Mandevu re-run on Thursday 5 November, leaving the UPND's Adrian Banda as the only candidate. Chisenga, the Tonse Alliance's man, says threats began on nomination day and spread to his family; the UPND said earlier this month it knew of no threats and that weak opponents should withdraw. The ECZ has not announced a declaration.

image.label: A ballot with one name
image.caption: Three of the four candidates in the Mandevu parliamentary by-election withdrew in letters dated 28 October 2026, a week before the 5 November poll.

body: The Mandevu parliamentary by-election, called after the 13 August vote in the Lusaka constituency was declared inconclusive, looks set to end without a vote. The Zambian Observer reported on Thursday evening that the three candidates standing against the UPND's Adrian Banda had each written to the Electoral Commission of Zambia to withdraw, in separate letters dated Wednesday 28 October. News Diggers reported on Friday morning that the Forum for Democracy and Development's Daniel Chisenga, who carried the Tonse Alliance ticket, had pulled out citing threats, and that the other two candidates had reportedly also withdrawn, leaving Banda unopposed.

The four had filed nominations on 8 October: Banda for the UPND, Chisenga for the FDD, Daniel Daka as an independent, and a Leadership Movement candidate whose first name both outlets give as Ntazana (the Observer prints the surname Muntungwa, News Diggers Musukuma). According to the Observer, Chisenga's letter gave no reasons, Daka asked to be excluded from the election without saying why, and the Leadership Movement candidate cited financial constraints. News Diggers reports that Chisenga says the threats to his life began on nomination day and later escalated to his family. The Observer noted that Banda's election unopposed will depend on the applicable procedure and formal confirmation by the ECZ; neither outlet reported a declaration by the Commission.

body.text: A campaign of allegation and denial

body: The threats were not a new claim. On 15 October the Tonse Alliance's secretary-general, Muhabi Lungu, told a press briefing that Chisenga had faced constant threats from people identifying themselves as UPND since filing his nomination and had not slept at home for three nights, News Diggers reported. The UPND's deputy secretary-general, Getrude Imenda, replied the next day that the party was not aware of any threats, challenged the alliance to name those responsible, and said that opponents who felt weak should withdraw rather than use the UPND's name. On 20 October she attributed a run of opposition withdrawals from by-elections to a lack of logistical support from their own parties.

body.text: Our candidate has been under constant barrage from people who have identified themselves as UPND.
body.attribution: Muhabi Lungu, Tonse Alliance secretary-general, at a press briefing in Lusaka on 15 October, as reported by News Diggers

body: Last week Lungu accused people in UPND regalia of disrupting the alliance's campaign in Mandevu, attacking members including Chisenga and abducting a woman, allegations News Diggers reported as unverified. Inspector-General of Police Graphel Musamba responded in a statement, reported by the paper on 24 October, that police would investigate every reported case of violence in the constituency, including the alleged attack on Chisenga, and had an electoral security plan in place for before, during and after the poll. No arrests had been reported by Thursday.

body.text: The third seat to go the same way

body: If the ECZ confirms the withdrawals, Mandevu will be the third contest on the 5 November slate decided without a vote. News Diggers reported on 20 October that the Commission had declared the UPND's Anderson Banda elected in the Lumezi parliamentary by-election (News Diggers calls the seat Lumezi North) after the NRPUP withdrew from all by-elections and the Leadership Movement's candidate resigned, and that the UPND's Felix Mulwanda would be declared Mayor of Mbala on 5 November after the Progressive Alliance Party's Pythias Sichitalwe pulled out. The Times of Zambia reported in September that the ECZ had set 5 November for the Mandevu and Lumezi parliamentary polls, the Mbala mayoralty and eleven ward seats, with nominations on 8 October and campaigning from 10 October to 18:00 on 4 November.

Mandevu itself is being re-run because of what happened on election night in August. The Zambian Observer recalled that the ECZ said the constituency's results-tallying centre was attacked, data transmission equipment destroyed and documents stolen, which it said rendered the process null and void. The constituency had been held by the UPND's Christopher Shakafuswa; Banda, who had entered as an independent, joined the UPND during its adoption process and was adopted ahead of Shakafuswa, the Observer says. Chisenga is a former Mayor of Lusaka.

body.confirmed: That four candidates were nominated for Mandevu on 8 October and polling is set for 5 November (Times of Zambia; News Diggers). That Chisenga has withdrawn, in a letter to the ECZ dated 28 October, citing threats (News Diggers; the Zambian Observer reports the letter but says it gave no reasons). That Tonse alleged threats and attacks and the UPND denied knowledge of them (News Diggers, 16–24 October).
body.unverified: That Daka and the Leadership Movement candidate have also withdrawn rests on the Zambian Observer's report of their letters; News Diggers says they have 'reportedly' withdrawn. The ECZ has not, in any report seen, declared Banda elected. Who made the threats Chisenga describes is not established; the police investigation announced last week has not reported.

stories.title: The last two desks filled: Milupi takes Transport and Logistics, Kalila takes Housing with an order that councils allocate only serviced land, and Mulusa returns as Chief Whip
stories.excerpt: A day after swearing in 24 ministers, President Hichilema completed the line-up on Thursday 29 October: Charles Milupi to Transport and Logistics, with instructions to move on the Lobito Corridor, TAZARA and Zambia Railways without delay, and Christopher Kalila to the new Ministry of Housing, told to tackle unplanned settlements by putting roads and sanitation in before plots are handed out. In Parliament the Speaker announced that Solwezi North's Stafford Mulusa is Government Chief Whip again, with Matero's Alexander Sakala as his deputy.

image.label: Transport and Housing
image.caption: Charles Milupi and Christopher Kalila were sworn in as Ministers of Transport and Logistics and of Housing at State House on Thursday 29 October 2026.

body: The two ministries left empty on Wednesday have ministers. President Hakainde Hichilema swore in Charles Milupi as Minister of Transport and Logistics and Christopher Kalila as Minister of Housing at State House on Thursday 29 October, according to a State House statement distributed through APO Group and carried by Africa Newsroom and Pan African Visions. News Diggers had reported on Thursday morning that the Transport and Housing posts were the only ones unfilled after Wednesday's swearing-in of 24 Cabinet ministers and ten provincial ministers under the 30-ministry structure Parliament approved on Tuesday.

Milupi takes a ministry whose brief the President framed around corridors. The statement says he asked the ministry to prioritise economic corridors so that transport infrastructure draws investment along key routes, and named three projects to be implemented without delay: the Lobito Corridor, the revitalisation of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority and the rehabilitation of Zambia Railways. He wants rail to carry more bulk cargo to relieve the roads and support mining, agriculture and trade, and he asked for private-sector partnerships and modernised logistics systems.

body.text: We are talking about services, investment, trade and growth to fulfil our goals and the agenda.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema at the swearing-in at State House on Thursday 29 October, in a statement issued by State House

body: Kalila's instructions were more specific. The President directed the new Housing Minister to deal with unplanned settlements through structured urban planning and basic infrastructure before land is allocated, and told local authorities to allocate only serviced land, meaning plots with roads, sanitation and other essential facilities already in place. He called for standardised, affordable housing designs for teachers, nurses and other public workers, arguing that standardisation cuts cost, and for modern building technologies and financing to widen home ownership. Kalila, in remarks reported in the same statement, put the national housing deficit at about 1.5 million units, rising to a projected 3 million by 2030, with the greatest need in rural areas, and linked decent housing to disease prevention. Milupi called transport the backbone of the economy and said plans were in place to lower logistics costs.

The President also returned to the theme of his Wednesday address, stressing accountability, integrity and collective responsibility, and that the national interest must come before personal interest. On Wednesday, News Diggers reported, he had warned the new ministers against laziness and what the paper called excessive happy hours, and urged them to stay humble.

In the National Assembly on Thursday, Speaker Nelly Mutti announced that she had received formal communication from the UPND appointing Stafford Mulusa, the Solwezi North MP, as Government Chief Whip and Alexander Sakala, the Matero MP, as Deputy Government Chief Whip, News Diggers reported on Friday. Mulusa held the Chief Whip's post from 2021, when Princess Kasune was his deputy; Kasune was later made a minister and replaced as deputy by Likando Mufalali in February 2025. The paper also noted the opposition's recent appointments: the NRPUP's Ezra Tembo as Leader of the Opposition, Milenge's Gystave Chonde as party whip and Nyimba's Paul Lungu as his deputy.

Thursday's two appointments fill the only posts News Diggers listed as vacant after Wednesday, so each of the 30 ministries created by Tuesday's realignment now has a named minister; Zambia Monitor's list of the 24 has Harry Kamboni at Education and Douglas Syakalima at Skills and Higher Education, Peter Kapala at Electricity and Makozo Chikote at Petroleum. No gazette notice had been seen by Friday morning. The first test of the full bench is the 2027 budget, now due on Friday 6 November.

stories.title: Inflation edges up to 6.3 per cent as diesel jumps 24 per cent in a month, and September's trade balance swings to a US$186 million deficit on weaker copper exports
stories.excerpt: ZamStats' October bulletin, released in Lusaka on Thursday 29 October, puts annual inflation at 6.3 per cent, up from 6.1, with food inflation easing to 5.7 per cent and non-food rising to 7.4. The price table explains why: diesel up 23.8 per cent and petrol up 24.4 per cent in a month, while a 25 kg bag of breakfast meal is a tenth cheaper than a year ago. Exports fell 8.1 per cent in September and imports rose 5.4 per cent, turning August's US$48 million surplus into a US$186.4 million deficit as refined copper earnings dropped 15 per cent.

image.label: 6.3 per cent
image.caption: ZamStats' monthly bulletin for October 2026, released on Thursday 29 October, shows annual inflation at 6.3 per cent and a September trade deficit of US$186.4 million.

body: Prices are rising a little faster, and the reason is not food. The Zambia Statistics Agency's monthly bulletin for October, presented in Lusaka on Thursday 29 October by General Statistician Sheila Mudenda, puts annual inflation at 6.3 per cent, up from 6.1 per cent in September and the second consecutive monthly rise, Zambia Monitor and the Maravi Post reported. Food and non-alcoholic beverage inflation eased to 5.7 per cent from 5.8 per cent, and is far below the 14.1 per cent of a year earlier. Non-food inflation rose to 7.4 per cent from 6.6 per cent. Mudenda attributed the increase in the headline rate mainly to price movements in non-food items.

The bulletin's own tables show where. Month on month, prices rose 0.7 per cent in October, against 0.4 per cent in September; non-food prices alone rose 1.2 per cent in the month. Transport inflation jumped to 10.8 per cent a year from 5.8 per cent, and the bulletin's national average prices record diesel at K33.25 a litre, up 23.8 per cent on the month, and petrol at K31.46, up 24.4 per cent, after October's fuel price increases. Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels ran at 7.6 per cent and health at 8.9 per cent. Food, by contrast, kept the headline down: a 25 kg bag of breakfast meal averaged K235.86, 10.2 per cent cheaper than in October 2025, and roller meal K181.99, down 11.8 per cent. A 20-litre tin of maize grain rose 5.2 per cent in the month but is still 11.9 per cent below a year ago.

Inflation is highest in Lusaka Province, at 8.6 per cent, up from 8.1 per cent, and Lusaka alone contributes 2.5 of the 6.3 percentage points; the Copperbelt, at 5.5 per cent, contributes 1.2. Rates fell in Eastern (4.6 per cent), Southern (5.4) and Western (5.0) provinces and rose everywhere else, with North-Western climbing from 5.0 to 5.8 per cent. Food contributed 3.4 points of the national figure and non-food 2.9, of which housing and utilities accounted for 0.9 and transport 0.7. The rate remains inside the Bank of Zambia's 6 to 8 per cent target band; the Monetary Policy Committee next meets on 25 and 26 November, Zambia Monitor noted in its currency report this week.

The same bulletin carries September's trade figures, and they are weaker. Exports fell 8.1 per cent to US$1,606.4 million while imports rose 5.4 per cent to US$1,792.8 million, so the balance moved from a surplus of US$48.0 million in August to a deficit of US$186.4 million. Refined copper earnings fell 14.9 per cent to US$934.7 million as volumes dropped 15.3 per cent to 64,900 tonnes, even though the LME price edged up to US$14,483 a tonne. Traditional exports were down 10.0 per cent and non-traditional exports 4.2 per cent. On the import side, capital goods rose 33.5 per cent. Over January to September, total trade is US$27.1 billion, 43.4 per cent more than in the same months of 2025, and cumulative refined copper exports are 663,000 tonnes, up 6.3 per cent.

The figures land in a nervous currency market. Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday that the kwacha closed at K20.30 to the dollar on 27 October, its weakest in twelve months by Access Bank's reckoning and 16.6 per cent down from K17.41 in June, with importers' dollar demand, September's 250-basis-point policy rate cut and the K19.9 billion supplementary budget all cited as pressures. An economist quoted by News Diggers on Thursday, Bright Chizonde, warned that borrowing about K18 billion of that supplementary budget on the domestic market could push up interest rates and crowd out private borrowers. The 2027 budget, which will set out next year's borrowing, is now due on 6 November.

stories.title: US$31 billion to 2050 and a US$23.1 billion hole for ZESCO: the Energy Ministry's financing strategy for the power plan, as the Permanent Secretary puts capacity at 4,722 MW
stories.excerpt: The Ministry of Energy's financing strategy for the Integrated Resource Plan, presented at a Centre for Trade Policy and Development meeting in Lusaka and reported by Zambia Monitor, says the plan needs about US$31 billion by 2050 and US$11.6 billion by 2030, roughly US$1.07 billion a year against concessional flows averaging US$231 million. Under an open-access market, ZESCO could face a gap of up to US$23.1 billion between 2033 and 2050. Separately, Permanent Secretary Arnold Simwaba put installed capacity at 4,722 MW, up from 3,777 MW in 2024.

image.label: The US$31 billion plan
image.caption: The Ministry of Energy's financing strategy for the Integrated Resource Plan puts the cost of expanding Zambia's power system at about US$31 billion by 2050.

body: Zambia's plan to more than quintuple its generating capacity by mid-century comes with a price tag, and a warning about who pays it. Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday 28 October that the Ministry of Energy's presentation on the financing strategy for the Integrated Resource Plan, delivered at a stakeholder meeting convened by the Centre for Trade Policy and Development at the Radisson Blu in Lusaka, puts the plan's total financing need at about US$31 billion by 2050, of which US$11.6 billion is needed by 2030. That is roughly US$1.07 billion a year, which the presentation says current financing cannot cover: bilateral and multilateral development banks have provided nearly half of the sector's funding, at an average of US$231 million a year.

The plan's targets are large. The presentation gives current capacity as 3,877 MW, rising to 10,013 MW by 2030 and 23,193 MW by 2050, with variable renewables, mainly solar and wind, growing from 7.9 per cent of installed capacity now to 33 per cent by 2030 and 56 per cent by 2050. Large hydro is 79.6 per cent of today's capacity, which the presentation identifies as the system's vulnerability to drought, as recent droughts have shown.

The strategy compares two ways of running the electricity market to 2050: the single-buyer model, in which ZESCO buys all power and sells it on, and an open-access model, in which generators and large customers can trade directly over ZESCO's wires. Under open access, Zambia Monitor reports, ZESCO could face a financing gap of up to US$23.1 billion between 2033 and 2050. The article does not give the single-buyer result, any tariff path or the utility's debt position, and it quotes no ZESCO or government official, so how the ministry proposes to close the gap, through tariffs, concessional debt, private capital or asset sales, is not reported.

On Tuesday, at a policy dialogue on the Population and Energy Nexus Study 2026, Energy Permanent Secretary Arnold Simwaba said installed national generation capacity now stands at 4,722 MW, up from 3,777 MW in 2024, News Diggers reported. He credited the reform programme pursued since 2021 with improving the investment climate, bringing in private generators and expanding generation, transmission and access. The two official figures, 3,877 MW in the IRP presentation and 4,722 MW from the Permanent Secretary, are not reconciled in either report; the difference may reflect the IRP's base year or what each counts as installed and available, and this edition has not been able to establish which.

The strategy arrives with new political owners. Zambia Monitor's list of the ministers sworn in on Wednesday 28 October has Peter Kapala as Minister of Electricity and Makozo Chikote as Minister of Petroleum, the two halves of the old Energy portfolio under the 30-ministry structure. The IRP's financing question is now theirs to answer, and the 2027 budget on 6 November is the first place they will have to.

stories.title: 1,622 cases and 30 deaths, more than half of them before reaching a clinic: Chilengi tells Parliament the outbreak has spread to 20 districts as 709,018 people are vaccinated
stories.excerpt: In a ministerial statement to the National Assembly on Thursday 29 October, Health Minister Roma Chilengi said Zambia had recorded 1,622 cholera cases and 30 deaths since 28 July, 16 of the deaths in communities before patients reached a health facility. The outbreak covers 20 districts in six provinces, Mumbwa and Chisamba the latest; Lusaka Province accounts for 1,090 cases. The Treasury has released K13 million for emergency water supply, and 709,018 people, 91 per cent of the target, have been vaccinated in Lusaka, Chibombo and Chongwe.

image.label: Thirty deaths
image.caption: Health Minister Roma Chilengi told the National Assembly on Thursday 29 October 2026 that the cholera outbreak had reached 1,622 cases and 30 deaths in 20 districts.

body: The cholera count that stood at 1,488 cases and 29 deaths on Wednesday has moved on. Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi told the National Assembly in a ministerial statement on Thursday 29 October that Zambia had recorded 1,622 cases since the outbreak was declared on 28 July, of which 228 are laboratory-confirmed, and 30 deaths, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers reported. Of the deaths, 16 occurred in communities before the patients reached a health facility and 14 in facilities. In the latest 24-hour period there were 74 new cases across 12 districts and no deaths; 104 patients were admitted and 1,488 had recovered and been discharged.

body.text: Of the 30 deaths recorded, 16 occurred in communities before the patients could reach a health facility.
body.attribution: Roma Chilengi, Minister of Health, in a ministerial statement to the National Assembly on Thursday 29 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: The outbreak now covers 20 districts in six provinces. Lusaka Province has 1,090 cases, Central 298, Luapula 133, Northern 88, Southern 11 and the Copperbelt 2. The newest districts to report cases are Mumbwa, with one, and Chisamba, with two. Zambia Monitor's report of the statement gives no district-level breakdown for Lusaka, where the capital has carried most of the national count throughout the outbreak.

Chilengi described a whole-of-government response. The National Epidemic Preparedness, Prevention, Control and Management Committee has been convened to coordinate across ministries. The Ministry of Finance and National Planning has released K13 million to the water and sanitation ministry for emergency safe water supply. Surveillance, case detection, laboratory confirmation, treatment and community prevention are being strengthened with provincial and district health offices, partners, community leaders and volunteers. On the volunteers, News Diggers reports that the minister argued that volunteering should not be tied to promises of employment and that the government does not need to promise volunteers jobs during an outbreak.

The vaccination campaign is nearly complete. The International Coordinating Group on vaccine provision approved 782,147 doses of oral cholera vaccine, and 709,018 eligible people aged one and above have received it, which the minister put at 91 per cent of the target: 555,472 in ten wards of Lusaka District, 134,699 in four wards of Chibombo and 18,847 in one ward of Chongwe. Vaccination continues in Lusaka Central and parts of Munali. Chilengi asked MPs to lead community mobilisation in their constituencies and to repeat the prevention messages: safe water sources, boiling or treating water of uncertain quality, handwashing with soap, proper sanitation, no open defecation and food hygiene.

The outbreak has roughly doubled in a fortnight. On 13 October the Zambia National Public Health Institute's update, reported by the Times of Zambia, put the cumulative count at 874 cases and 23 deaths in 13 districts of five provinces; Thursday's figures are 1,622 and 30 in 20 districts of six. The absence of deaths in the latest 24 hours and the 91 per cent vaccine coverage in the worst-affected wards are the government's grounds for saying the response is working; 74 new cases in a day shows transmission has not stopped. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, drawing on Africa CDC data to 11 October, counted 1,773 cases and 37 deaths in Zambia for the whole of 2026, which includes cases from before the current outbreak was declared.

stories.title: Mapatizya falls vacant: the High Court at Livingstone nullifies Emeldah Munashabantu's election over the ECZ's handling of the count, finds the MP blameless and awards costs
stories.excerpt: Judge Kazimbe Chenda has set aside the 13 August election of the UPND's Emeldah Munashabantu in Mapatizya, Zimba District, on the petition of independent Clive Miyanda, the Zambian Observer reported on Thursday evening, citing Mwebantu. The judgment is reported to dismiss the misconduct allegation against the MP but to find that the ECZ did not conduct the post-voting process substantially in accordance with electoral law after violence at the Kabanga totalling centre. The ECZ is to pay the petitioner's costs. An appeal is open.

image.label: Mapatizya, vacant
image.caption: The High Court sitting in Livingstone is reported to have nullified the election of Mapatizya MP Emeldah Munashabantu on Thursday 29 October 2026 over irregularities in the post-voting process.

body: A UPND seat won by 482 votes in August has been nullified, according to a report on Thursday evening. The Zambian Observer, citing Mwebantu, reported that Judge Kazimbe Chenda, sitting at Livingstone, has set aside the election of Emeldah Munashabantu as Member of Parliament for Mapatizya, in Zimba District, on the petition of the independent candidate Clive Darius Miyanda. The Electoral Commission of Zambia was the second respondent. Mwebantu's own report, headlined that Mapatizya is now without an MP, could not be read by this desk, which has relied on the Observer's account of the judgment; no other outlet had reported the ruling by Friday morning.

As reported, the judgment separates the two grounds of the petition. The allegation of misconduct against Munashabantu was dismissed, because none was proved. The allegation of procedural irregularity, particularly in what happened after voting closed, succeeded. The court is reported to have found that the ECZ did not conduct the post-voting electoral processes substantially in accordance with the electoral laws, and that while violence at the Kabanga totalling centre affected the petitioner and both respondents alike, it was the irregular steps taken by the Commission's agent afterwards that triggered the petition. On costs, the ECZ is to pay Miyanda's, to be taxed if not agreed, and Munashabantu, found blameless in the Commission's conduct, bears only her own.

News Diggers reported from the trial in September that Miyanda, represented by Chizai Zulu of Linus and Partners, alleged irregularities including that results from seven polling stations had been swapped. The ECZ's witness, the constituency returning officer Newton Mudenda, testified that the declared result was valid: 14,812 votes for Munashabantu to 14,330 for Miyanda. The Commission also argued that the GEN 20 result forms Miyanda filed were not valid because they were not accompanied by the other required documents. The Observer's report does not say which of these specific allegations the court accepted beyond the post-voting process at Kabanga.

A nullification by the High Court may be appealed to the Constitutional Court, and until any appeal is decided or the time to appeal passes the seat is not formally vacant; the Speaker then declares the vacancy and the ECZ sets a by-election. Neither Munashabantu nor the UPND had been reported as announcing whether they will appeal. The ruling arrives in a week in which, as reported above, the ECZ's conduct of the August count in Mandevu is also the reason that constituency is going back to the polls.

body.confirmed: That a petition by Clive Miyanda against Munashabantu's election was tried before Judge Kazimbe Chenda at Livingstone, with the declared result 14,812 to 14,330 (News Diggers, September). That the Zambian Observer, citing Mwebantu, reported on 29 October that the court has nullified the election, dismissed the misconduct ground and ordered the ECZ to pay costs.
body.unverified: This desk has read one account of the judgment. The judgment itself, the date it was delivered and any reaction from Munashabantu, the UPND or the ECZ have not been seen. Whether an appeal will be lodged is unknown. The reported finding against the ECZ concerns its agent's conduct of the post-voting process; it is not a finding of wrongdoing against the MP, who was expressly found blameless.

sources.title: Livingstone High Court has nullified the UPND's Mapatizya Parliamentary seat held by Emelda Munashabantu

stories.title: A final in Baku: Zambia's under-15s beat Slovakia 3–1 and Senegal 4–3 in one day and meet Portugal for the Tier B title on Friday, with Maxen Msimuko on 13 goals
stories.excerpt: Two knockout wins on Thursday 29 October took the Junior Chipolopolo to the Tier B final of the first FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival. Slovakia were beaten 3–1 in the quarter-final, and in the semi-final Zambia came from behind three times against Senegal, Moses Munkombwe, Maxen Msimuko twice and Samuel Musonda scoring in a 4–3 win, ZamFoot reported. Msimuko has 13 goals in the tournament and Musonda scored one and set up two in the semi. The final against Portugal is at the Crystal Hall on Friday 30 October, one of four finals with an African side.

image.label: Zambia v Portugal
image.caption: Zambia's under-15 boys reached the Tier B final of the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku on Thursday 29 October 2026 and face Portugal on Friday.

body: The comeback against England on Wednesday turned out to be a rehearsal. On Thursday 29 October Zambia's under-15 boys played two knockout matches in Baku and won both, ZamFoot reported: a 3–1 quarter-final win over Slovakia and then a 4–3 semi-final against Senegal in which they trailed three times. They will play Portugal in the Tier B final at the Crystal Hall on Friday 30 October, AfricaSoccer reported, one of four finals at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival that will feature an African team.

The semi-final was the match of the tournament for Zambia. ZamFoot's account has Senegal ahead early from close range past goalkeeper Patrick Mudenda, and Kafue Celtic's Moses Munkombwe levelling three minutes later from a Samuel Musonda pass. Senegal went ahead again against the run of play; Maxen Msimuko equalised with a solo goal. In the second half Msimuko conceded a penalty, Senegal converted, and Zambia were behind for a third time at 3–2. Musonda, of Sporting Lusaka, then found Msimuko's run into the box for 3–3, Msimuko's 13th goal of the tournament, and Musonda himself scored the winner from a rebound off a Msimuko effort. Msimuko finished with two goals; Musonda with one goal and two assists. ZamFoot did not name the scorers against Slovakia.

Zambia finished second in their group, behind the group winners who went into Tier A, after four wins in five matches, including a 13–0 defeat of Montserrat. In Tier B's round of 32 on Wednesday they beat England 3–2 after trailing 2–0, with Msimuko, Musonda and Chrispine Katoba scoring, and in the round of 16 the same day they beat Niger 2–0 through Benson Bwalya and Msimuko, according to a COSAFA round-up carried by AllAfrica. That makes six knockout goals for Msimuko across Wednesday and Thursday and 13 in all.

The tournament is unlike any the country's youth teams have played. It has 189 teams playing eight-a-side matches of 40 minutes; after the group stage the teams were sorted into six tiers, so that no team's tournament ended with a defeat. Only Tier A decides the world title. Tier B is the second rank, and Zambia's opponents in it have included England, Niger, Slovakia and Senegal. Portugal reached the final after knocking out South Africa 2–1 in the round of 16, the COSAFA round-up noted.

AfricaSoccer lists the four finals with African interest: Zambia against Portugal in Tier B, Tunisia against Belarus in Tier C, the Central African Republic against Bangladesh in Tier E and Ethiopia against New Zealand in Tier F. Madagascar, the other COSAFA side to reach the Tier B quarter-finals, were drawn against Senegal in that round, so Zambia's semi-final opponents had come through them. A kick-off time for the Tier B final was not given in the reports seen by this desk; the COSAFA round-up says the tier finals are at Baku's Crystal Hall on Friday 30 October. The result will be in Saturday's edition.

stories.title: Maniema Union, Singida Black Stars and a club still to be decided: Red Arrows learn their Confederation Cup group, with the first matches from 27 November
stories.excerpt: The draw in Cairo on Wednesday 28 October put Red Arrows in Group C of the TotalEnergies CAF Confederation Cup with AS Maniema Union of DR Congo, Singida Black Stars of Tanzania and the winner of an unresolved qualifier among CR Belouizdad, AS Douanes and Hafia. It is the Zambian champions' first group stage in the competition, reached by beating Kaizer Chiefs on penalties. The group stage opens on the weekend of 27 to 29 November and ends in late January, with the top two in each group going to the quarter-finals in February.

image.label: Group C
image.caption: Red Arrows were drawn into Group C of the 2026/27 CAF Confederation Cup in Cairo on Wednesday 28 October 2026, alongside Maniema Union and Singida Black Stars.

body: Red Arrows know most of their opponents. The draw for the group stage of the 2026/27 TotalEnergies CAF Confederation Cup, held in Cairo on Wednesday 28 October, placed the Zambian champions in Group C with AS Maniema Union of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Singida Black Stars of Tanzania, CAF announced in a statement carried by AllAfrica and ZamFoot reported. The fourth team is not yet known: CAF says CR Belouizdad of Algeria, AS Douanes of Mauritania and Hafia of Guinea are competing for a place still to be confirmed, which the reports attribute to an outstanding qualifying matter rather than a replay.

It is the first time the Lusaka club has reached the group phase of the competition, ZamFoot noted. They got there by holding Kaizer Chiefs of South Africa to a 1–1 aggregate draw and winning the penalty shoot-out.

Group A has Al Ahly of Egypt, Raja Casablanca of Morocco, ASKO Kara of Togo and Primeiro de Agosto of Angola. Group B has Morocco's Royal Armed Forces, Tanzania's Azam, Libya's Al Ahly Tripoli and South Africa's Durban City. Group D has USM Alger, CS Sfaxien of Tunisia, Black Bulls of Mozambique and Real Bamako of Mali. The first round of group matches is on the weekend of 27 to 29 November, the last at the end of January 2027, and the top two in each group go to the quarter-finals in February. ZamFoot called Arrows' group competitive but not insurmountable.

Arrows' home matches depend on the stadium question. ZamFoot reported on Thursday that CAF has given the National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka temporary Category 3 approval for November, after an assessment from 19 to 22 October, covering the national team's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Burundi on 13 November and the under-23s' Olympic qualifier against Burkina Faso on 15 November, while raising concerns the association must address before a further assessment. FAZ general secretary Charles Chakatazya said the assessment confirmed the stadium meets the key requirements for CAF and FIFA matches. Whether the approval extends to Arrows' first home group match at the end of November was not addressed in the reports seen. Match dates and venues for Group C have not been published.

stories.title: Six for Senegal: a judoka, a badminton player, three swimmers and a sprinter carry Zambia into the first Olympic event held in Africa, which opens in Dakar on Saturday
stories.excerpt: The Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games open on Saturday 31 October and run to 13 November. Zambia's team, sent off at the Senegalese embassy in Lusaka on 25 October, is Elisha Zimba in judo, Bhardwaj Anjuman in badminton, Sibongile Miti, Joshua Mulenga and Edward Cole in swimming and Nathan Matete in athletics, with Besa Chibwe as chef de mission. The National Olympic Committee says it applied for 115 places and was allocated six, and that Zambia has won four medals, one of them gold, at three previous Youth Games.

image.label: Dakar 2026
image.caption: Six Zambian athletes compete at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Senegal, the first Olympic event held in Africa, from 31 October to 13 November 2026.

body: The first Olympic event ever staged in Africa opens in Dakar on Saturday 31 October, and Zambia will be there with six athletes. The National Olympic Committee of Zambia named the team at a send-off at the Senegalese embassy in Lusaka on Sunday 25 October: Elisha Zimba in judo, Bhardwaj Anjuman in badminton, Sibongile Miti, Joshua Mulenga and Edward Cole in swimming, and Nathan Matete in athletics. The Youth Olympic Games run until 13 November.

Six is a small team, and the NOCZ explained why. It applied for 115 athlete places, it said, and received six through the quota process run by the international federations, the IOC and the host, which allocates places by sport rather than by country. The four coaches are Ian Stephenson for swimming, Donald Mabo for badminton, Chipoma Mulenga for athletics and Ndungu Mwitumwa for judo. Besa Chibwe is chef de mission, with Monica Lombe as deputy, with a games administrator, welfare officer, physiotherapist, doctor and press attaché completing the delegation.

In a speech read by vice-president Nakaonga Kakoma, NOCZ president Alfred Foloko said Zambia had won four medals at three previous Youth Olympic Games, one gold, two silver and one bronze, and expressed confidence that the six would represent the country with honour. The acting Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, Gibson Muyaule, who officiated, called the Games a historic milestone for the continent and urged the athletes to behave as ambassadors and to observe anti-doping rules. Senegal's consul-general, Sow Maguette, described the Games as Africa's chance to show it can host major international events, and NOCZ secretary-general Boniface Kambikambi told the athletes the Games were about experience and friendship as much as medals.

body.text: We have confidence in these young athletes and believe they will represent Zambia with honour.
body.attribution: Alfred Foloko, NOCZ president, in a speech read at the team's send-off at the Senegalese embassy in Lusaka on Sunday 25 October, as published by the NOCZ

body: For Zambia the three swimmers are the largest contingent, and the places are spread across four sports and four coaches for six athletes. Competition schedules by sport are published by the organisers; the NOCZ had not, by Friday, published its athletes' individual event dates, and this desk will carry results as they are reported.

sources.title: Team Zambia Officially Sent Off Ahead of Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games

analysis.title: What 5 November will actually decide, and what it will not
analysis.body: The bail hearing has now consumed four sittings without a word of argument, and the court's reported warning that it will rule on the papers if either side is not ready changes the incentives. The State's affidavit is already filed; the applicants' reply is already filed. On 5 November the judges can decide on documents alone, which means neither side can buy more time by not being ready. The question before them is narrow: whether detention of about ten weeks without a trial date, on charges that carry life imprisonment, violates the applicants' constitutional rights enough to require release or bail. The State's case is that treason and terrorism investigations take time and that two months is short by the standards of the cases it cites; the applicants' case is that investigating after charging is not a lawful reason to hold anyone. Whatever the court decides, it will not decide guilt. A grant of bail does not weaken the charges; a refusal does not strengthen them. The dates for the substantive petition, which the court says will follow the bail ruling, are where the case itself begins. What to watch on the day is whether the State opposes a ruling on the papers, and whether the court sets those dates.

analysis.title: Three seats, no votes: what unopposed means in Mandevu, Lumezi and Mbala
analysis.body: If the ECZ confirms the withdrawals, the November by-elections will have produced two MPs and a mayor without a ballot being cast. The two accounts of why are not reconcilable from the reporting so far. The UPND's position, stated before the Mandevu letters were written, is that opposition parties cannot fund campaigns and that candidates leave when the support does not come; one of the three Mandevu withdrawals is reported to cite exactly that. The Tonse Alliance's position is that its candidate was threatened from nomination day, and his withdrawal letter, as News Diggers reports it, says the threats reached his family. The police promised an investigation on 23 October and have reported nothing since. Both things can be true of different candidates, and neither has been tested. What is testable is procedure. The ECZ has not yet declared Mandevu, and how it does so matters: the Mbala and Lumezi declarations followed the same route, and the Commission's conduct of the August count is the reason Mandevu is voting again at all. The other open question is Mapatizya, where a court has reportedly just found the Commission's post-voting conduct wanting in a different constituency. A by-election there would be the next test of whether contests in Zambia are still decided at the ballot box.

analysis.title: A fuel-driven 6.3 per cent lands on a budget that is still being written
analysis.body: The October numbers are not alarming on their own: 6.3 per cent is inside the Bank of Zambia's target band and food inflation is still falling. The composition is the point. Non-food inflation jumped from 6.6 to 7.4 per cent in a month because diesel and petrol rose by roughly a quarter after October's fuel price increases, and transport inflation nearly doubled. That is a one-off step up in the price level, but it is also exactly the kind of pass-through that a weaker kwacha, now around K20.30 to the dollar, feeds. The September trade deficit, driven by a 15 per cent drop in refined copper earnings, shows the other channel. Two decisions sit in the next four weeks. The budget on 6 November will say how much of the K19.9 billion supplementary spending and next year's deficit is to be borrowed at home, which economists quoted this week argue pushes up interest rates. The Monetary Policy Committee on 25 and 26 November will decide whether September's 250-basis-point cut still fits a currency at a one-year low and non-food prices accelerating. The case for holding is strong on today's data; the case for reversing is not yet made. November's figures, with a full month of the new fuel prices, will be the ones that matter.
